A 44-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of headache, dizziness, and imbalance. He had a history of hypertension and cervical disc herniation. One year ago, he underwent transcatheter closure for patent foramen ovale. His father had progressive cognitive decline and imbalance since the age of 50 years and died of cerebral hemorrhage at the age of 65 years.

Neurological examination revealed brisk bilateral tendon reflexes and bilateral Babinski sign.

- Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI):    Image 1 Title: Axial Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Brain    Image 1 Description: T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery showing lacunar infarctions and periventricular white matter hyperintensities (WMH)    Image 2 Title: Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging    Image 2 Description: Showing a lobe-dominant distribution of multiple cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and relatively fewer CMBs in deep regions, mainly involving bilateral parieto-occipital lobes  - Genetic Analysis:    Revealed a heterozygous mutation (c.754G>A, p.A252T) in the HTRA1 gene

A 24-year-old white man presented with an 8-month history of persistent swelling around his left eye. He had no history of significant acne vulgaris or rosacea and no visual symptoms. He had been evaluated by an allergist and an ophthalmologist and had not improved with corticosteroid ophthalmic solutions or oral antihistamines. On examination, there was non-erythematous, non-pitting edema of the left periorbital region without conjunctival inflammation. Paranasal radiography and maxillofacial CT scans showed only periorbital soft-tissue swelling. Patch testing with the North American Standard Series was negative, and a tuberculin skin test result was negative. A skin biopsy revealed numerous dermal ectatic blood vessels and lymphatics with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate.

clinical_record:
A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Adverse Local Tissue Reaction (ALTR) associated with metal-on-metal hip arthroplasty

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.
